Heavenly Citizenship
HEV-un-lee SIT-ih-zun-ship
phrase (biblical expression)
From Philippians 3:20, “For our conversation is in heaven”; the Greek politeuma denotes commonwealth, citizenship, or seat of government—the believer's true country lying in heaven.

📖 Biblical Definition

Heavenly citizenship is the truth that the believer's true commonwealth, home, and allegiance lie not on earth but in heaven, whence he looks for the Saviour. The word the Apostle uses, rendered “conversation” in the Authorized Version, signifies a citizenship or commonwealth; the saint is enrolled as a citizen of a heavenly country and lives on earth as a pilgrim and stranger. His politics, his loyalties, and his hopes are governed from above. This pilgrim character runs through all Scripture: Abraham “looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God”; the patriarchs “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.” The believer, set down for a season in this world, holds it loosely, knowing he has here no continuing city but seeks one to come. His citizenship shapes his conduct: he walks worthy of the heavenly calling, sets his affection on things above, and refuses to be conformed to the present age. And his citizenship fixes his hope, for “from thence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ: who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body.” The pilgrim's journey ends not in dissolution but in resurrection glory, when the King shall come to bring His scattered citizens home to the city whose builder and maker is God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The believer's true commonwealth and home in heaven, which governs his conduct and fixes his hope while he sojourns on earth.

HEAVENLY CITIZENSHIP, phrase (biblical expression). From Philippians 3:20; the Greek politeuma, commonwealth or citizenship.

The believer's enrollment as a citizen of the heavenly country, with allegiance and hope fixed above.

The pilgrim character of the Christian, who sojourns on earth as a stranger seeking a city to come.

As recorded in Scripture: “For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).

By extension, the governing motive for holy conduct and the ground of the saint's hope of resurrection.

📖 Key Scripture

Phi 3:20 — "For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ:"

Heb 11:13 — "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off, and were persuaded of them, and embraced them, and confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth."

Col 3:1 — "If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God."

1Pe 2:11 — "Dearly beloved, I beseech you as strangers and pilgrims, abstain from fleshly lusts, which war against the soul;"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though its pilgrim hope is dulled wherever the church sinks its affections wholly into this present world.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The phrase is not the prize of any ideological campaign, yet the truth it carries is steadily eroded by a worldliness that treats earth as the believer's home and heaven as a distant rumor. When the church loses the sense of pilgrimage, it grasps after earthly security and forgets the city which hath foundations.

The principle to recover is the pilgrim's posture. Heavenly citizenship is no excuse for idleness or for despising the duties of earthly life, for the saint serves faithfully in his calling; but it forbids him to set his heart below. He holds the world loosely, sets his affection on things above, and waits for the Saviour from heaven. So living, he walks worthy of the heavenly calling and is ready for the day when Christ shall fashion his lowly body like unto His glorious body.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase draws on the language of commonwealth and pilgrimage that runs from the patriarchs to the Apostle.

expand to see more

Politeuma means a commonwealth or seat of citizenship, the believer's true country.

Philippians 3:20 names heaven as that commonwealth and Christ as the awaited Saviour.

Hebrews 11 paints the patriarchs as strangers and pilgrims seeking a heavenly city.

Colossians 3 commands the risen believer to seek the things that are above.

First Peter 2:11 binds the pilgrim identity to abstinence from fleshly lusts.

Usage

"The phrase teaches believers to hold earthly things loosely as pilgrims bound for heaven."

"Preachers use it to fix the church's hope on the return of Christ from heaven."

"It motivates holy conduct, for the citizen of heaven walks worthy of his calling on earth."
